Conjura is built on one bet: that AI can be used as far as it will go in mathematical research, provided what comes out is held to a standard that does not care where it came from.

This page has two halves. [Where Conjura is headed](#part-i-where-conjura-is-headed) is the roadmap, and changes as the work does. [The reasoning underneath](#part-ii-the-reasoning-underneath) is slower-moving: why a badge can look worse than a result deserves, why a wrong conjecture stays up, why a name goes on a review the way it goes on a paper.

# Part I: where Conjura is headed

## Two problems

### Research that collides instead of compounding

Progress in cryptographic research is often slowed by more than mathematical difficulty: uncoordinated effort and opaque tooling slow it down too. Results get produced in isolation, so partial progress is rediscovered more than once, and the same dead ends get walked into by people who never find out about each other's attempts.

Conjura's answer is a public, durable record: what's been tried, what's resolved, what's still stuck, and by whom, so that compute and attention can be pointed at open problems collaboratively instead of redundantly.

### How the field publishes AI-assisted work

The second problem carries the same weight as the first, and it is one the field has made for itself.

Start with what the policies actually say, because the honest reading is not the convenient one. Read at source on 16 August 2026, they converge on something reasonable rather than on a ban:

| | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **IACR** ([Crypto 2026](https://crypto.iacr.org/2026/aipolicy.php), [Asiacrypt 2025](https://asiacrypt.iacr.org/2025/aipolicy.php), [TCC 2026](https://tcc.iacr.org/2026/aipolicy.php)) | Each says it will "generally follow the ACM Policy on the use of AI tools". Graduated disclosure: none for grammar, a footnote for a sentence, an appendix naming tools, versions and prompts for whole generated sections. No AI author. |
| **ACM** ([policy FAQ](https://www.acm.org/publications/policies/frequently-asked-questions)) | Generative AI "cannot be listed as authors on ACM Works under any conditions". AI used in *conducting the research* must be described in the methods section. AI used in *writing the manuscript* no longer requires disclosure. |
| **IEEE** ([author guidelines](https://journals.ieeeauthorcenter.ieee.org/become-an-ieee-journal-author/publishing-ethics/guidelines-and-policies/submission-and-peer-review-policies/)) | AI-generated content "shall be disclosed in the acknowledgments section", the system named and the affected sections identified with "a brief explanation regarding the level at which the AI system was used". Editing and grammar are outside the intent. |

No AI authorship, humans accountable for everything in the paper, substantive generation disclosed. None of that is unreasonable, and Conjura does not argue with any of it.

Two things are worth noticing all the same.

The first is a limit on **degree**. The clause ACM states, and the IACR venues reproduce, is that a work must be "not primarily the result of the tool's generative capabilities". That is the line this site crosses deliberately: several results here are primarily a model's output, directed and then checked by a person. "Primarily" has no operational definition, no reviewer can recover it from a finished manuscript, and none of the three policies describes a way to detect a breach or a consequence for one.

The second is **drift**. The IACR pages present ACM's graduated disclosure ladder for generated text, while ACM's own current FAQ says writing assistance no longer requires disclosure at all. Whichever reading is right, a rule that three sibling venues state differently from the body they defer to is a guideline, not a standard.

So the disagreement is not "they forbid AI and we allow it", which would be false and easy to check. It is about what disclosure *is*. At a venue it is a sentence in an acknowledgements section: unverifiable, unenforced, attached to a paper judged whole. Here it is per artifact and machine-checked. A [status badge](/open-problems/status-legend/index.qmd) grades what has been verified and cannot claim more, an attribution field records who or what produced each part, the [prompts](/prompts/index.qmd) are published in full, and a CI gate fails the build when a page and its formal artifact drift apart. Session logs are the one part not yet delivered, recorded above rather than glossed.

Same principle. Taken seriously enough to build gates around it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Policies as read on 16 August 2026, at the URLs above. All three have revised their wording more than once, so the vintage matters. The IACR and IEEE pages were fetched directly; acm.org returned HTTP 403 to an automated request, so its FAQ was read through a text-extraction proxy of the same URL.
:::

## What we're building toward

### Working in the open

We explore open conjectures in public rather than in private notebooks, sharing intermediate states as they happen. A recorded dead end saves someone else the time of rediscovering it; a partial result shared early is something someone else can build on now rather than years later.

The intent is that every result is published with the prompts, tools and session logs that produced it. That is partly an integrity commitment, and partly incidental: a public record of how current AI tools actually perform against unresolved problems is data the field does not otherwise have.

Two of the three are in place. The [prompts](/prompts/index.qmd) are published in full, and every statement, proof and formalization carries an attribution field saying whether a human or a model produced it. The third is not. Each statement folder has a `sessions/` directory for the raw transcript, and as of 16 August 2026 **every one of them is empty**: nothing on the site is currently backed by the session that produced it. That gap stays written here until it closes.

Working in the open has one deliberate exception, for results that could break something deployed. It is narrow, and set out in [publishing in the open, and the one exception](#publishing-in-the-open-and-the-one-exception).

### Rigour, and the exposition that makes it usable

Where feasible we favour machine-checked proofs over informal write-ups, and precise, minimal statements over padded ones. A proof a machine has checked carries a different kind of confidence than one that merely reads convincingly, and the site is built to keep that distinction visible rather than blur it.

Formal artifacts alone do not make a result understood, so we keep the informal explanation of why a result is true and why it was hard alongside them. That is usually most of what makes a result worth reading.

### Who gets to do the work

Two of the ideas below are mechanisms for this. The principle belongs first, because otherwise they read as unrelated engineering.

Access to capable models is now a real input to research output, and it is not evenly held. A well-funded group can run an expensive search across several models for weeks; someone on a personal subscription cannot. To the extent that results start to track available compute, the field's output starts to track budgets rather than ideas, and it does so invisibly, because nobody publishes the attempts they could not afford to run.

That is a poor direction for a field whose central claim on anyone's attention is that its results are checkable by anyone.

Conjura redistributes no compute today, and should not be read as claiming otherwise. What it does do, and has not named as such until now, is give its tooling away: the [prompts](/prompts/index.qmd) behind the results here are published in full, for anyone to take and point at their own problems. That is a small levelling act and currently the only one in effect.

### Ideas we're exploring

None of the four below is built. They are directions, not features, and saying so plainly matters more than the pitch.

**Bounties on open problems.** Erdős placed cash bounties on conjectures he found interesting. A modern decentralized version would let anyone attach an on-chain bounty to an open problem, claimable without an intermediary once a resolution is verified.

**Idle tokens.** Plenty of people and organizations hold API credits or subscription capacity they never use in full. That capacity could be pointed at Conjura's backlog, resolving conjectures, checking write-ups, formalizing proofs, instead of expiring unused.

**Distributed, multi-model compute.** Some problems here are demanding enough that no single account, and no single model, is the right unit of work. A system Conjura ran itself could orchestrate one task across several accounts and several models, rather than serializing it behind one rate limit or one model's blind spots.

**A journal of AI-assisted research.** Stated plainly, because it is what the rest of this page implies: cryptology should have a venue for work that is openly and substantially AI-assisted, judged on whether its results survive checking rather than on the model's share of the drafting. The IACR already publishes [Communications in Cryptology](https://cic.iacr.org/), a real and well-run venue, and this is not a complaint about it. It is a difference of posture: CiC carries the same ACM-derived policy as the conferences, so a paper that is primarily model-generated has no natural home there however thoroughly it was verified. What such a venue needs is mostly what this site is already building, and whether it becomes a journal, a track, or a body of work that makes the case by existing, we do not know.

And to have some fun doing it.

# Part II: the reasoning underneath

## Embrace it, and keep it in check

Everything else in this half is an instance of one commitment, and the rest reads more easily if the commitment is stated first.

Conjura's posture toward AI is dual. Use these tools as far as they will go, and hold what comes out to a standard that does not care where it came from. Neither half stands alone. Enthusiasm without checking produces work that reads as rigorous and has been verified by nobody, which is the failure the field is right to fear. Checking without enthusiasm keeps the standard and forgoes the capability, at the moment the capability is arriving.

The two are not in tension, and that is the point. Adoption is what makes rigorous checking necessary; rigorous checking is what makes adoption defensible.

The sections that follow are that commitment applied to particular decisions, and are best read as its instances rather than as separate principles: a badge that can understate but never overstate, a wrong conjecture that keeps its page, an attribution rule that changes the record but never the standard, and verification treated as work worth crediting. The last of them turns the same commitment on the roadmap in the first half of this page.

## Plausible isn't the same as true

AI has made it cheap to produce mathematical writing that reads as rigorous without anyone, human or machine, having checked it. Writing more carefully does not fix that: a fabricated citation can be written as carefully as a real one. So the site tracks what has actually been checked, machine-verified or independently human-reviewed, separately from what merely reads well, and lets a badge say "not yet checked" rather than borrow the authority of work nobody did. A badge here is deliberately narrow: it can say less than a result deserves, never more than what was verified.

## A negative result is still a result

A withdrawn statement keeps its page as a tombstone; a disproof of an easy special case is filed as `research-solved` rather than left off as an embarrassment. Quietly deleting a wrong conjecture is understandable and is exactly what causes the rediscovery this site exists to prevent: someone else pays, in time, for every unrecorded dead end. A record that shows only successes is a highlight reel, not a record of progress.

## Attribution doesn't erase the work

Whether a human or an AI produced a statement, a proof, or a review, the record says so, and either way the thing produced is checked to the same standard. This isn't a hedge against AI-generated work being wrong. It's the same rigor applied regardless of source, which is the only way a badge can mean the same thing twice. Passing that check is what should earn confidence, not who or what attempted it.

This is the exact point of difference with the venue policies in the first half. They ask how much of the work the model did, a question with no measurable answer and no enforcement. Conjura asks what has been checked, which has both.

## Verification is a job, and it's been an undervalued one

Reviewing a proof, or checking that a formalization matches the statement it claims to formalize, has never carried the reward that producing a result does: a byline is visible, a careful review that finds nothing wrong is not. The site designs against that asymmetry rather than accepting it: agentic stress-testing before a human sees a submission, a reviewer's name permanently attached to what they checked, formal artifacts wherever feasible rather than only where convenient.

That stress-testing shouldn't come from one model either. A single model's blind spots, applied to both the writing and its own review, are still just one perspective wearing two hats; the same conjecture and proof are worth putting in front of more than one model, and more than one account, for the same reason a paper is worth putting in front of more than one human reviewer.

## Publishing in the open, and the one exception

Everything above argues for publishing: prompts, attribution, dead ends, wrong conjectures, partial progress as it happens. There is one case where Conjura does not, and it is worth naming rather than leaving as an unstated caveat, because it genuinely conflicts with the rest.

If a result breaks something deployed, publishing it hands an attack to whoever reads the page first. Nearly nothing here is in that category: conjectures, lower bounds and asymptotic statements in idealized models have nothing to exploit. But it is not empty, and the site's own defaults sharpen it. An agent working a conjecture cannot tell in advance whether it is producing a separation or a practical break, and under a publish-everything rule it would publish the break, with a reproduction, before any person read the output.

So [responsible disclosure](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/SECURITY.md) is a named exception, not a silent one. Three things keep it from swallowing the principle it interrupts.

It suspends **when**, never **whether**. Nothing in scope is withheld permanently or quietly dropped, and the eventual write-up carries the same badge, attribution and checking as anything else.

The scope is written down and deliberately narrow: a break of a deployed scheme, a parameter set or standard whose concrete security is worse than claimed, or an attack on a named implementation. Asymptotic and model-level results, which are the normal case here, do not trigger it.

And the embargo has to hold somewhere real. This repository is public and every branch in it is readable, so an embargoed result does not sit unmerged on a branch; it stays out of the repository entirely until release. A policy that relied on a merge gate would be decoration, and saying so plainly is the same commitment as the rest of this page.

## This site has not been reviewed either

The two sections above apply to the research artifacts: a statement, a proof or a Lean file each carries a graded provenance and a line saying who checked it. Nothing covers the container.

The prose on every page, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the schema, the scripts under `scripts/`, the templates, the encyclopedia stubs and this page itself were generated by an AI. A human directed, prompted and refined all of it throughout, so it is not unsupervised output, and the responsibility for it is not deferred anywhere by saying so. But it has not had thorough independent review by anybody, and it should have, from more than one reviewer.

That is stated here for the same reason the badges exist. A site arguing that provenance and review status belong on every artifact, while saying nothing about the provenance and review status of itself, would be making the most quotable and most fair criticism available to a reader. Better to write it down.

**What takes this notice down.** Not time, and not more edits. It narrows as review actually happens, in the same shape as a badge: when a part of the site has been independently reviewed, this section says which part, by whom, and when, and the claim shrinks to what remains unreviewed. When nothing substantive is left unreviewed, the section goes. Until then it stays exactly as broad as it currently is, because a notice that quietly softens without anything having been checked is worse than no notice.

## Say plainly what isn't built yet

An idea worth exploring and a feature that exists are different things, and Conjura would rather mark the gap between them explicitly than let a roadmap read as more finished than it is. That discipline is part of the same worldview as the rest of this page: the badge, the tombstone, the attribution rule, and an honest "this isn't built yet" are all the same underlying commitment, applied to a different part of the site.

It applies to the first half of this page too, which is why everything under [ideas we're exploring](#ideas-were-exploring) is marked unbuilt in one place rather than pitched four times. The compute-fairness argument above is likewise a principle the site holds, not a programme it runs. Naming an ambition is not delivering it, and a page arguing for honesty about AI would be a poor place to blur that.
